sources.title: Dolly Parton, one of country music's most singular performers, has died at age 80 (NPR)
Dolly Parton dies after brief battle with cancer, according to publicist (WSMV Nashville)
Dolly Parton, country music icon, dead at 80 (Global News)
Dolly Parton dies at 80 | Special Report (video, CBS News)

chunks.text: Dolly Parton, the [[queen]] of American [[country music]], {{passed away}} on Tuesday, August 25, in Nashville, Tennessee. She was 80 years old. Her team said she died after a short [[battle]] with [[cancer]], surrounded by [[loved ones]]. Only days earlier, she had told a magazine that she had {{put off}} dealing with her own health while she {{looked after}} her husband, who died last year after nearly 60 years of [[marriage]].

verbs.correct: To die, said in a gentle way
verbs.wrong: To faint for a few moments
verbs.why: Newspapers say a beloved actor passed away, and families say grandpa passed away peacefully. Parton passed away in Nashville with her loved ones around her.

verbs.wrong: To finish work ahead of time
verbs.why: People put off homework, dentist visits, and hard conversations. Parton admitted she had put off dealing with her own health for too long.

verbs.correct: To care for a person who needs help
verbs.wrong: To search for a lost item
verbs.why: Grandparents look after the kids, and nurses look after patients through the night. Parton looked after her sick husband instead of watching her own health.

chunks.text: Her story sounded like one of her songs. Parton {{grew up}} poor in the mountains of Tennessee and {{started out}} singing as a young girl. She {{broke through}} to national fame in the late 1960s and never stopped, writing [[classics]] like "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors," and "I Will Always Love You." She reached pop fans with "Here You Come Again" and the theme from the movie "9 to 5," and {{went on}} to act in films like "Steel Magnolias." She won 10 Grammy Awards, and her records sold more than 100 million copies around the world.

verbs.wrong: To move to a new city
verbs.why: You can grow up on a farm, grow up bilingual, or grow up surrounded by music. Parton grew up poor in the mountains of Tennessee, and she sang about it forever.

verbs.correct: To begin a career or journey
verbs.why: Many stars start out in tiny clubs, and some companies start out in a garage. Parton started out singing as a young girl long before the world knew her name.

verbs.correct: To reach success after a struggle
verbs.wrong: To take a break from music
verbs.why: Young athletes dream of breaking through, and small bands break through with one hit. Parton broke through in the late 1960s and stayed on top for decades.

verbs.correct: To continue with the next thing
verbs.wrong: To rest between two long tours
verbs.why: A student can go on to medical school, and a runner can go on to the next race after one win. After she became famous for her music, Parton went on to act in movies like 'Steel Magnolias.'

chunks.text: Parton was more than a singer. She built the [[theme park]] Dollywood in the Smoky Mountains, which brings visitors from around the world to her [[home region]]. Through her Imagination Library, she {{gave away}} free books to children every month from birth to age five. She also {{stepped in}} during the pandemic, giving one million dollars to [[medical research]] that helped create a Covid vaccine. Her [[charity]] work made her loved far beyond music. She often said she simply wanted to {{give back}}.

verbs.correct: To hand out things for free
verbs.wrong: To sell tickets at the door
verbs.why: Stores give away samples, and rich founders sometimes give away their fortunes. Through her library program, Parton gave away millions of children's books.

verbs.correct: To act when help is needed
verbs.why: A referee steps in to stop a fight, and a neighbor steps in when a family struggles. Parton stepped in during the pandemic with a million dollars for research.

verbs.correct: To return help to your community
verbs.wrong: To borrow money from a bank
verbs.why: Athletes give back by coaching kids, and graduates give back to their old schools. Parton said her books and gifts were her way to give back.

chunks.text: The [[tributes]] came quickly. The president ordered [[flags]] [[lowered]] and said there had never been anyone like her. Radio stations across Tennessee played her [[signature song]] at the same moment, and [[stars]] from country and pop remembered her as a [[legend]]. Fans around the world shared their [[grief]] online. There will be no big public [[funeral]]. [[At her request]], only close family will attend a small private [[service]]. Her music, her park, and her books will {{carry on}} without her, and her songs will still {{bring together}} fans of every kind.

verbs.wrong: To pack for a long journey
verbs.why: A family business can carry on for generations, and traditions carry on after their founders. Her park, her books, and her music will carry on without her.
Big games bring strangers together, and family recipes bring generations together. Her songs brought together country fans, pop fans, and everyone in between.

mainIdea.s: A beloved country music star died of cancer at 80, days after saying she had ignored her health while nursing her husband. Fans and leaders honored a life of music and giving.
mainIdea.why: She passed away in Nashville after a short battle with cancer, and tributes came from the president to radio stations.

mainIdea.s: One of country's greatest voices died at 80 after a long illness that she had discussed publicly for years. Her family announced a huge public funeral at her famous theme park.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the cancer battle was short and mostly private, and she asked for a small family service, not a public funeral.

mainIdea.s: A famous country singer announced at 80 that cancer is forcing her to retire from touring forever. She plans to spend her remaining years running her library charity full time.
mainIdea.why: This is not a retirement story. The singer passed away on August 25, and others will carry on her projects.
